opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there's a lot of value there. The general base model gives you a broad foundation: language understanding, reasoning, world knowledge, coding ability. Then for a particular domain, whether that's healthcare, law, chip design, or a specific scientific field, you can take that foundation and specialize it with domain data. You often get something quite a bit better in that area than the general model, without paying the cost of training from scratch.

We've seen this with things like Med-PaLM and the medical work built on Gemini. Starting from a strong general model and then adding medical data, and evaluation by clinicians, gets you a big jump in quality on those tasks. And you still keep a lot of the general capabilities, so the model can explain things clearly, handle follow-up questions, and reason across topics.

I do think there's an interesting tension, though. As the general models get more capable, some of the gap a domain-specific model was closing shrinks, because the base model has already absorbed a lot of that knowledge. So the question becomes: what does the specialization really buy you? Often it's data the general model has never seen, like proprietary data, very recent data, or very specialized data, or it's tighter behavior: the formatting, safety constraints, or style that a domain needs.

Longer term, I'd like to see more modular approaches. Imagine one large model with pieces that are specialized for different domains, where you only activate the relevant parts for a given request, and you can update or add a specialist module without retraining everything. That gives you a lot of the benefit of domain specialization while still sharing all the general knowledge underneath. So I think domain-specific models are valuable today, and the way we build them will probably become much more fluid and composable over time.

r001.rationale: It describes specializing a general base model by adding domain data, including medical data, which conveys enriching the model with data from that domain.

r002.rationale: It says specialization can improve performance in a domain and that general capabilities are often retained. It does not state that increasing one domain’s representation can reduce capabilities in other domains.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there's a lot of value there, and the reason is that a general model like Gemini has already absorbed an enormous amount about the world. It knows language, it knows how to reason, it knows a fair bit of chemistry and law and medicine. So when you want a model that's really good at, say, interpreting medical images, or helping with cybersecurity, or education, you're not starting from scratch. You're starting from a model that already understands most of what it needs to, and you're nudging it toward a particular distribution of problems.

Med-Gemini is a nice example. We took the general Gemini models and did additional training on medical data, clinical reasoning, radiology reports, that kind of thing, and the performance on medical benchmarks went up quite a bit over the base model. But the thing that's interesting is that you keep most of the general capability. The model can still talk to a patient in plain language, it can still write code if you need it to, it just also happens to be much better at the medical stuff. If you tried to train a medical-only model from scratch, you'd need way more medical data than exists, and you'd lose all that general grounding.

The other thing I'd say is that the base model keeps improving, and the domain-specific work rides along with it. Every time we get a better Gemini, the starting point for the specialized version gets better too, and often the amount of extra work needed shrinks. Sometimes capabilities that required a specialized model a year ago are just there in the general model now.

So I tend to think of it as a spectrum rather than a binary. There's the general model, there's lightweight adaptation like prompting or tool use or small amounts of fine-tuning, and then there's deeper domain training when the stakes are high and the data is available. Over time my guess is that more and more moves toward the general end, but there will always be areas, especially ones with specialized data or regulatory requirements, where it's worth going deeper.

r001.rationale: The response says domain-specific training adds data from that domain and nudges the model toward its particular distribution.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that greater representation of one domain can weaken other capabilities; it instead says the specialized model keeps most general capability.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of value in that approach. A general model gives you a foundation with broad capabilities—understanding language, writing code, reasoning about different kinds of problems. And then you can build on that with domain-specific data and training to make it more useful in a particular setting.

Medicine is a good example. You want the broad understanding, but you also want the model to understand medical terminology, interpret the kinds of information clinicians work with, and perform well on the particular tasks you care about. That requires careful evaluation with people who understand the domain.

And sometimes specialization doesn’t mean changing the model’s weights. It might mean giving it access to the right information or connecting it to tools. So I think there’s a spectrum here, from a general model with good context to a more deeply specialized model. The question is which combination gives you the reliability, quality, and efficiency you need for that application.

r001.rationale: It says a general model can be built on with domain-specific data and training to improve its usefulness in a particular setting.

r002.rationale: It does not state that increasing a domain’s representation in training data can improve that domain while reducing capabilities in other domains.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of value in that approach. A general model gives you a foundation: it understands language, it can reason across different kinds of information, and it has fairly broad knowledge. You can then build on that with domain-specific data, tools, and training to make it much more useful for a particular set of problems.

Take medicine, for example. You want broad capabilities, but you also need the model to understand specialized terminology, interpret the kinds of inputs clinicians work with, and meet a much more demanding standard of evaluation. That specialization can make a real difference.

The interesting question is how much belongs in the model itself versus what you provide through context or access to external information. You don’t necessarily want to retrain a model every time a fact changes. So I think you’ll see a combination: strong general models, some domain-specific adaptation, and connections to the information and tools needed for the task.
